props.title: Society
props.initialSlug: Rich teen uncovers high society's horrific secret

sections.content: Society stands as one of body horror's most audacious social satires. Director Brian Yuzna crafted a wickedly smart critique of Reagan-era upper class excess, following teenager Bill Whitney as he uncovers his wealthy family's grotesque secret. The film builds like Blue Velvet (1986), peeling back suburban perfection to reveal corruption, but explodes into a surreal finale featuring the "shunting" - still one of practical effects wizard Screaming Mad George's most disturbing achievements. This sits alongside They Live (1988) and Parents (1989) as peak 80s horror commentary on class warfare.

sections.content: The film's genius lies in how it builds dread through social anxiety before unleashing its grotesque metaphors. Like Return of the Living Dead (1985) and Night of the Creeps (1986), it wraps serious themes in outrageous gore effects. But where those films targeted middle America, Society specifically skewers the ultra-wealthy Beverly Hills elite. The prosthetic effects in the climactic shunting scene - where the rich literally feed on the poor - remain unmatched in their ability to disgust while making a clear political statement. SUBHEAD: Class Horror & Social Commentary

Society kicked off a wave of horror films directly addressing class warfare. People Under the Stairs (1991) showed predatory landlords literally feeding off the poor, while Candyman (1992) explored urban legends through the lens of class and racial divisions. More recently, films like Get Out (2017) and Ready or Not (2019) have picked up Society's torch, using horror to expose elite predation of the underclass. The film's influence can even be seen in Parasite (2019), where class warfare plays out in a wealthy home's architecture.
